power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Over recent decades, advances in neonatal and perinatal care have substantially improved outcomes for infants born very preterm (VPT), defined as birth before 32 weeks of gestation 1 .
text.formatted: Over recent decades, advances in neonatal and perinatal care have substantially improved outcomes for infants born very preterm (VPT), defined as birth before 32 weeks of gestation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: As survival has increased and severe early morbidity has declined, attention has progressively shifted towards the longer-term consequences of VPT birth 2 .
text.formatted: As survival has increased and severe early morbidity has declined, attention has progressively shifted towards the longer-term consequences of VPT birth <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Clinical care and research have traditionally prioritized acute complications, growth, and respiratory, neurological, sensory, and motor outcomes 3 , while the assessment of cognitive and functional outcomes has remained largely concentrated in early childhood.
text.formatted: Clinical care and research have traditionally prioritized acute complications, growth, and respiratory, neurological, sensory, and motor outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> , while the assessment of cognitive and functional outcomes has remained largely concentrated in early childhood.

text.text: However, the consequences of VPT birth extend well beyond this period, with potential implications for mental health and social functioning across the life course.

This should not be a surprise as there is abundant evidence from multiple neuroimaging studies of widespread, heterogenous, alterations in brain structure and function after preterm birth. 4 Furthermore, the outcomes most often prioritised in research and clinical care do not always align with the concerns of people born VPT and their families.
text.formatted: This should not be a surprise as there is abundant evidence from multiple neuroimaging studies of widespread, heterogenous, alterations in brain structure and function after preterm birth. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> Furthermore, the outcomes most often prioritised in research and clinical care do not always align with the concerns of people born VPT and their families.

text.text: A recent analysis of social media discourse around prematurity identified a divergence between professional and lived-experience narratives: healthcare professionals focused predominantly on survival, neonatal complications, growth, and physical health outcomes, whereas people born preterm and their families more often described emotional difficulties, disrupted social experiences and identity formation, educational and occupational challenges, and the lasting psychological impact of VPT birth 5 .
text.formatted: A recent analysis of social media discourse around prematurity identified a divergence between professional and lived-experience narratives: healthcare professionals focused predominantly on survival, neonatal complications, growth, and physical health outcomes, whereas people born preterm and their families more often described emotional difficulties, disrupted social experiences and identity formation, educational and occupational challenges, and the lasting psychological impact of VPT birth <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: This divergence is also reflected in the outcomes prioritised in research and clinical follow-up.
Readily quantifiable outcomes, such as sensory impairment, major neurodevelopmental disability, or healthcare use, have come to define the recognized burden of prematurity 6 .
text.formatted: Readily quantifiable outcomes, such as sensory impairment, major neurodevelopmental disability, or healthcare use, have come to define the recognized burden of prematurity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: By contrast, emotional wellbeing, social functioning, identity, participation, and longer-term mental health are assessed less consistently and therefore remain less visible within both research and care.

Despite this lack of visibility, there is now consistent evidence that people born VPT are at increased risk of a broad range of neurodevelopmental, emotional, and psychiatric difficulties throughout their life.
Compared with those born full term (FT), they are more likely to experience cognition, learning, and executive function difficulties 7 .
text.formatted: Compared with those born full term (FT), they are more likely to experience cognition, learning, and executive function difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: They also show greater levels of internalizing symptoms, including anxiety, low mood, and peer difficulties 8 , alongside problems with behavioural and emotional regulation 9 and a higher prevalence of autism 10 , attention-deficit / hyperactivity disorder 11 , and psychotic-like experiences 12 .
text.formatted: They also show greater levels of internalizing symptoms, including anxiety, low mood, and peer difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , alongside problems with behavioural and emotional regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> and a higher prevalence of autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> , attention-deficit / hyperactivity disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> , and psychotic-like experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Beyond clinical symptoms and diagnoses, differences are also evident in broader social and functional outcomes.
People born VPT may have more difficulty forming friendships and romantic relationships 13 , progressing through education, finding and maintaining employment, and living independently 14 .
text.formatted: People born VPT may have more difficulty forming friendships and romantic relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , progressing through education, finding and maintaining employment, and living independently <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: These vulnerabilities may persist into adolescence and adulthood, with population-based studies reporting increased rates of psychiatric disorders, specialist mental healthcare use, and psychiatric hospitalization [15] [16] [17].
text.formatted: These vulnerabilities may persist into adolescence and adulthood, with population-based studies reporting increased rates of psychiatric disorders, specialist mental healthcare use, and psychiatric hospitalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: These outcomes are heterogeneous and should not be interpreted as inevitable consequences of preterm birth 18 .
text.formatted: These outcomes are heterogeneous and should not be interpreted as inevitable consequences of preterm birth <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Risk is higher, however, among those born at earlier gestational ages, those who experience greater neonatal morbidity, and those exposed to social adversity, and difficulties may also occur in the absence of major neurological disability.
Some may only become apparent as academic, social, and emotional demands increase at school entry, during adolescence, or in the transition to adult life 19, 20 .
text.formatted: Some may only become apparent as academic, social, and emotional demands increase at school entry, during adolescence, or in the transition to adult life <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: Early developmental assessment therefore provides only a partial picture of later functioning, while early difficulties do not necessarily predict poor outcomes in adolescence or adulthood.
Despite this life-course pattern of vulnerability, specialised follow-up after VPT birth remains concentrated in early childhood.

In England, NICE recommends enhanced multidisciplinary developmental surveillance for children at highest risk, culminating in a detailed assessment at 2 years of corrected age, with an additional developmental assessment at 4 years for children born before 28 weeks of gestation 21 .
text.formatted: In England, NICE recommends enhanced multidisciplinary developmental surveillance for children at highest risk, culminating in a detailed assessment at 2 years of corrected age, with an additional developmental assessment at 4 years for children born before 28 weeks of gestation <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: Thereafter, most children return to universal child-health surveillance.

In the United States, the American Academy of Pediatrics similarly recommends enhanced developmental surveillance for children born preterm, but longer-term monitoring is largely embedded within routine paediatric primary care 22 .
text.formatted: In the United States, the American Academy of Pediatrics similarly recommends enhanced developmental surveillance for children born preterm, but longer-term monitoring is largely embedded within routine paediatric primary care <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Although this framework is important for identifying early developmental difficulties, specialised follow-up therefore typically ends well before many mental health problems become clinically apparent 23.
text.formatted: Although this framework is important for identifying early developmental difficulties, specialised follow-up therefore typically ends well before many mental health problems become clinically apparent <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref>.

text.text: Once neonatal follow-up ends, responsibility becomes dispersed across primary care, schools, paediatrics, and mental health services, with no single professional retaining oversight of the child's developmental trajectory and no consistent mechanism for reassessment at key transitions.
Families may be left to recognise emerging problems and navigate fragmented services themselves.

At the same time, prematurity may lose clinical salience: gestational age and neonatal history are not routinely incorporated into later mental health assessments 24, 25 , and new symptoms may be understood as isolated difficulties rather than as part of a broader developmental formulation.
text.formatted: At the same time, prematurity may lose clinical salience: gestational age and neonatal history are not routinely incorporated into later mental health assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> , and new symptoms may be understood as isolated difficulties rather than as part of a broader developmental formulation.

text.text: The gap is therefore broader than discontinuity in clinical surveillance: it also includes limited awareness, fragmented routes back into care, and few mechanisms through which people born preterm and their families can access information, mutual support, and reassessment when new difficulties emerge.
Other pediatric conditions offer useful models for addressing health consequences that may emerge long after the initial medical event.

Survivors of childhood cancer, for example, may receive risk-adapted follow-up into adolescence and adulthood, based on the recognition that physical, neurocognitive, psychological, and social late effects can become apparent years after treatment 26 .
text.formatted: Survivors of childhood cancer, for example, may receive risk-adapted follow-up into adolescence and adulthood, based on the recognition that physical, neurocognitive, psychological, and social late effects can become apparent years after treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: A similar life-course approach is increasingly evident in complex congenital heart disease.

Lifelong, age-appropriate cardiological follow-up is well established, including dedicated adult congenital heart disease services, while professional guidance increasingly recognises the need to consider neurodevelopmental and psychological outcomes across the life course, recognising that difficulties in learning, behaviour, emotional functioning, social participation, and independence may evolve as developmental demands change 27, 28 .
text.formatted: Lifelong, age-appropriate cardiological follow-up is well established, including dedicated adult congenital heart disease services, while professional guidance increasingly recognises the need to consider neurodevelopmental and psychological outcomes across the life course, recognising that difficulties in learning, behaviour, emotional functioning, social participation, and independence may evolve as developmental demands change <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: These models illustrate an important principle: when an early-life medical condition is associated with delayed or evolving psychological consequences, surveillance need not end once immediate physical risks have subsided or early developmental milestones have been achieved.

Translating a life-course perspective into practice does not require continuous specialist follow-up for every child born VPT, but rather access to professionals who recognise the potential long-term consequences of prematurity and can provide appropriate assessment and support when needed 29 .
text.formatted: Translating a life-course perspective into practice does not require continuous specialist follow-up for every child born VPT, but rather access to professionals who recognise the potential long-term consequences of prematurity and can provide appropriate assessment and support when needed <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: A feasible approach would combine anticipatory guidance, targeted reassessment at key developmental transitions, proportionate surveillance, and opportunities for peer support and shared experience among people born preterm and their families.

Families should be informed that attentional, emotional, social, or behavioural difficulties may become apparent beyond the preschool years and should receive clear guidance on when and how to seek reassessment.

Gestational age and neonatal history should also remain visible within health records and be routinely considered in developmental and mental health assessments at least throughout childhood and adolescence.

Children and young people with established neurodevelopmental difficulties, significant neonatal complications, social adversity, or early psychological symptoms may require more intensive monitoring, whereas others may need only anticipatory guidance and periodic review.
Schools also have an important role.

Awareness of a child's gestational age and neonatal history may help teachers interpret emerging learning, attentional, social, or emotional difficulties in context rather than viewing them simply as behavioural or academic problems.

Timing of school entry is one practical area in which this information may matter, particularly for children born very preterm whose chronological age at school entry may not fully reflect their developmental maturity.
Schools should also have clear routes for raising concerns and facilitating reassessment when difficulties emerge as educational and social demands increase.
The aim is not to pathologise prematurity, but to ensure that emerging difficulties are identified early enough for timely, proportionate, and effective support.
Closing this gap will also require a shift in how the long-term consequences of VPT birth are studied and represented within healthcare.

Research should move beyond survival and early neurodevelopmental impairment to examine mental health, social participation, educational and occupational functioning, and other outcomes identified as important by people born VPT and their families 5 .
text.formatted: Research should move beyond survival and early neurodevelopmental impairment to examine mental health, social participation, educational and occupational functioning, and other outcomes identified as important by people born VPT and their families <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: At the service level, prematurity should remain visible as a relevant developmental risk factor beyond discharge from neonatal follow-up 30 , with clear routes back to assessment when difficulties emerge.
text.formatted: At the service level, prematurity should remain visible as a relevant developmental risk factor beyond discharge from neonatal follow-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , with clear routes back to assessment when difficulties emerge.

text.text: The goal is not to create lifelong specialist surveillance, but to ensure continuity of developmental information across services as children move between neonatal care, primary care, schools, paediatrics, and mental health services, with explicit opportunities for reassessment when new concerns arise.
Advances in neonatal care have transformed survival after VPT birth.

The challenge now is to ensure that this success is matched by an equally ambitious approach to long-term outcomes, ensuring that people born VPT are not lost to follow-up when the consequences of prematurity emerge later in life.
